title: Mathematical Foundations — linear algebra, probability, and dynamics intuition
goal: The shared substrate under everything else in the vault: linear algebra powers state-space control, FOC's rotating transforms, and least-squares regression; probability powers sensor fusion, uncertainty analysis, and all of data-science-ai; ODE intuition powers every dynamics model from pendulum to QDD. This tree teaches the GEOMETRY first (transforms, projections, flow fields) with formulas as bookkeeping — each node cross-references where it lands in the mechatronics and DS trees. Threshold arcs: matrix-as-transform, Bayes inversion.

la-vector-space.claim: A vector is anything you can add to another and scale — arrows in space are just the picture. A basis is a minimal set whose combinations reach every point; dimension counts how many. Coordinates are always relative to a chosen basis: change the basis, change the numbers, same vector.
la-vector-space.probe: A friend says 'a vector IS an arrow with x and y components.' Correct the two errors: what actually defines a vector, and what are components? Then explain what it means for two vectors to span a plane and when they'd fail to.
rubric: vector defined by add/scale operations; arrow is one representation
components are coordinates RELATIVE to a basis — different basis gives different numbers for the same vector
two non-parallel vectors span the plane; parallel (or zero) vectors collapse to a line/point

viz.hint: Drag two basis vectors; watch any point's coordinates update as the grid shears with them.

la-vector-space.transfer_probe: One color is RGB (255, 0, 0), CMYK (0, 100, 100, 0), or just 'warm red' — same color, different numbers. Map basis, dimension, and basis-relative coordinates onto color systems: what is the basis in each, and why do the numbers change while the color doesn't?

la-matrix-as-transform.claim: A matrix is not a grid of numbers — it is a FUNCTION on space: it takes every vector and moves it somewhere. The columns tell you everything: column i is where the i-th basis vector lands. Read matrices as transforms and multiplication, determinants, inverses all become obvious pictures instead of procedures.
la-matrix-as-transform.probe: Given M = [[0,-1],[1,0]], predict where î=(1,0) and ĵ=(0,1) land WITHOUT computing anything, name the transform, and explain why this reading habit makes matrix multiplication feel natural rather than arbitrary.
rubric: î → (0,1), ĵ → (-1,0): columns ARE the images of basis vectors
the transform is 90° rotation (counterclockwise)
multiplication composes transforms — 'apply B then A' — which is why AB ≠ BA: rotation-then-shear differs from shear-then-rotation

viz.hint: Type matrix entries; watch the grid deform live — basis arrows land exactly on the columns.

la-matrix-as-transform.transfer_probe: Open your FOC/state-space notes: find one matrix there, read its columns as 'where the axes go', and say in words what physical operation it performs on signals or states.

la-matrix-compose.claim: Matrix multiplication is composition of transformations applied right-to-left: (AB)x means first B, then A. Each entry is a dot product — row meets column — which is exactly 'how much does A's output direction respond to B's input direction'. Associativity is free (composition chains); commutativity generally fails.
la-matrix-compose.probe: Explain why (AB)C = A(BC) is obvious once you think in transforms, then construct (or describe) two 2×2 matrices where AB ≠ BA, saying physically what each order does.
rubric: both groupings apply the same three transforms in the same order — grouping is bookkeeping, order is meaning
example pair: rotation vs shear/reflection — e.g. rotate 90° then flip horizontal ≠ flip then rotate
entry (i,j) = row_i(A) · col_j(B): measures alignment between A's output rows and B's input directions

practice.problem_frame: Compose two named transforms in both orders and predict/explain the difference.
practice.discriminates_from: Assuming commutativity; applying matrices left-to-right visually.
practice.verify: Track one basis vector through both orders by hand.

la-determinant.claim: The determinant measures how a transform scales AREA (2D) or VOLUME (3D): |det|=2 doubles areas, det=0 collapses space onto a line/point (information destroyed — irreversible), negative det flips orientation (mirror). It is the single number that reports whether a transform keeps the space full-dimensional.
la-determinant.probe: Without computing, what does det = 0 tell you about a transform's invertibility and about the system Ax=b having solutions? What does det < 0 mean geometrically? Compute det([[2,1],[4,2]]) and say what the value reveals.
rubric: det=0: space collapsed to lower dimension → inverse impossible → Ax=b has either no solution or infinitely many
negative determinant = orientation reversal (mirror flip)
det = 2·2 − 1·4 = 0: columns (2,4) and (1,2) are parallel — rank 1, collapse onto a line

viz.hint: Deform unit square with matrix sliders; area readout IS the determinant, flipping sign on mirror.

la-inverse-solve.claim: Solving Ax=b asks 'which input lands on b?' — the inverse A⁻¹ undoes the transform, so x = A⁻¹b exists only when nothing was destroyed (det≠0). Numerically you rarely compute A⁻¹ explicitly; solvers undo the transform directly, but the mental model stays: solve = reverse the mapping.
la-inverse-solve.probe: Your friend computes A⁻¹ by hand then multiplies to solve Ax=b and asks why the software doesn't do the same. Explain the conceptual role of A⁻¹, why software avoids forming it, and what happens conceptually when b lies outside the transformed space's image.
rubric: A⁻¹b reverses the transform to recover the unique pre-image — conceptually the definition of solving
forming A⁻¹ costs more and amplifies rounding error; LU/QR factorizations undo A more cheaply and stably
if det=0, some b have no pre-image (no solution) and others have infinitely many — the question itself breaks

la-eigen-decomp.claim: Eigenvectors are the directions a transform does NOT rotate — only stretch, by their eigenvalue. Av = λv. Complex eigenvalues mean rotation (pairs = spiraling planes); repeated/degenerate cases need care. Eigen-decomposition reveals a transform's true skeleton: independent stretching along special axes — which is why stability analysis and vibration modes are eigen-stories.
la-eigen-decomp.probe: For A=[[3,1],[0,2]], verify v=(1,0) is an eigenvector and give its eigenvalue. Then explain: what does a NEGATIVE eigenvalue do visually, and what does a complex pair mean for a dynamical system?
rubric: negative eigenvalue: direction preserved but FLIPPED through the origin (reflection+scale)
complex pair = rotation embedded in the transform — in dynamics, oscillation/spiral around equilibrium

viz.hint: Scatter trial vectors through a transform; only the eigen-directions stay on their own lines.

la-orthogonality-projection.claim: The dot product measures alignment: a·b = |a||b|cosθ — positive same-ish direction, zero perpendicular, negative opposed. Projection decomposes any vector into 'how much along here' + 'the remainder': proj = (a·b̂)b̂. Orthogonal bases make coordinates trivially readable and are why Fourier/PCA/regression all work by projection.
la-orthogonality-projection.probe: Compute the projection of b=(3,4) onto a=(1,0) and onto â=(1/√2, 1/√2). Then explain why orthogonal bases make 'reading off coordinates' trivial compared to oblique ones.
rubric: onto (1,0): component 3 → (3,0); onto diagonal: (3+4)/√2 ≈ 4.95 along â (accept 4.9–5.0)
projection formula: (a·b/|a|²)a — 'shadow' of b on a's line
orthogonal basis: coordinate = single dot product (no cross-coupling); oblique bases require solving coupled equations

viz.hint: Drag b around a fixed axis; watch shadow length track cosθ and vanish at perpendicular.

la-least-squares-geometry.claim: Least-squares regression has a pure geometry: Ax=b usually has NO exact solution (b off the column space), so you project b onto the column space — the closest reachable point — and the residual b−Ax̂ is orthogonal to that space. 'Best fit line' is really 'shadow of b on the plane spanned by your features'.
la-least-squares-geometry.probe: With 10 data points but 2 parameters, why can Ax=b be unsolvable, and what does least squares do about it? State the orthogonality condition the residual satisfies and connect it to why residuals-in-a-good-fit look structureless.
rubric: 10 equations, 2 unknowns → b generically outside the 2D column space → no exact solution exists
least squares finds x̂ minimizing ‖b−Ax‖: project b onto column space
residual ⊥ every column (Aᵀ(b−Ax̂)=0 — the normal equations); leftover signal in residuals means missed structure

viz.hint: Point b outside a plane; drop the perpendicular — the foot is the regression answer.

la-svd-intuition.claim: Every matrix, however messy, factors as rotate–stretch–rotate: SVD UΣVᵀ finds the input directions (V) that map to orthogonal output directions (U) with stretch factors σ₁≥σ₂≥…. The singular values rank importance: tiny σᵢ directions contribute almost nothing, which is exactly how compression, denoising, and pseudo-inverse discard junk.
la-svd-intuition.probe: An image is stored as a huge matrix. Explain in SVD language how keeping only the top-k singular values compresses it, what information gets thrown away, and how you'd pick k by looking at the singular value plot.
rubric: keep top-k stretch directions, truncate the rest: image ≈ Σᵢ≤k σᵢ uᵢvᵢᵀ — low-rank approximation
discarded: the small-σ directions, which after truncation mostly carry noise/fine detail
pick k at the elbow/cliff of the σ plot — where remaining values stop mattering

viz.hint: Slider adds singular terms back into a blurred image; watch structure return in σ-order.

prob-sample-space.claim: Probability lives on a sample space — the complete list of outcomes — with events as subsets: P(event) = favorable measure over total. All errors trace to a wrong sample space: missing outcomes, unequal weights treated as equal, or double-counting overlapping events. Define the space first; the arithmetic is then bookkeeping.
prob-sample-space.probe: Two fair coins are flipped. A friend says 'P(two heads, one head, two tails) = 1/3 each'. Diagnose the sample-space error, write the correct space, and recompute P(exactly one head).
rubric: outcomes aren't equally likely: HH, HT, TH, TT is the equiprobable space (ordered)
'one head' = {HT, TH} — two of four outcomes
P(one head) = 1/2; friend conflated outcome-counts with event-probabilities

prob-conditional.claim: Conditioning shrinks the world: P(A|B) recomputes probability inside the universe where B already happened — denominator restricted to B's region. Every conditional statement carries hidden scope: '70% accurate' means nothing until you ask 'accurate GIVEN what population?'
prob-conditional.probe: A test detects a fault 99% of the time when present and false-alarms 5% of the time. Restate both numbers as conditional probabilities with explicit conditions. Why can't you average them into one accuracy number?
rubric: P(positive | fault) = 0.99 (sensitivity); P(positive | no fault) = 0.05 (false-alarm rate)
they condition on DIFFERENT universes (fault-present vs fault-absent) — averaging them mixes populations
which matters depends on the base rate of faults — bridge requires Bayes
prob-conditional.transfer_probe: A spam filter advertises '99% accurate'. Accurate GIVEN what? Name the two universes (spam-world vs inbox-world), say which denominator your morning inbox actually lives in, and why the headline number misleads.

prob-bayes.claim: Bayes' rule runs conditioning backwards: from P(evidence|hypothesis) to P(hypothesis|evidence) — prior × likelihood, renormalized. The base-rate lesson is structural: rare hypotheses stay improbable even after strong-seeming evidence, because the prior multiplies everything. Testing positive is evidence ABOUT the test AND the hypothesis together.
prob-bayes.probe: Fault rate is 1-in-1000; the detector catches 99% of faults with 5% false alarms. A unit tests positive. Walk Bayes numerically: prior, likelihoods, posterior. Then explain in words why the posterior is still small despite the '99% accurate' test.
rubric: false alarms from the HUGE healthy population swamp the true positives from the tiny faulty one
structural lesson: evidence strength must fight the base rate; 'accuracy' numbers without priors mislead

viz.hint: Population grid of 10000 dots colored by truth; test-positive filter highlights how false alarms dominate.

prob-bayes.transfer_probe: Pick a real diagnostic in your builds (a sensor reading suggesting a wiring fault). Estimate its base rate and error rates, and compute whether one alarm should convince you.

prob-independence.claim: Independence means knowledge changes nothing: P(A|B) = P(A), equivalently P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B). It is a STRONG assumption that real systems violate constantly — shared causes induce correlation without direct links. Assuming independence when events share a driver is the standard way probability models lie.
prob-independence.probe: Two sensors both measure motor temperature. Their readings agree closely. A friend claims 'two independent sensors agreeing confirms the temperature'. Attack the independence assumption: what shared failure modes break it, and what would genuinely independent confirmation require?
rubric: shared drivers: same calibration batch, same wiring loom, same ambient conditions, same firmware bug — any of them correlates the errors
agreement of correlated instruments certifies the COMMON cause, not the quantity
genuine independence needs different physics/channels: e.g. thermistor vs IR pyrometer on separate supply rails

prob-random-var-expectation.claim: A random variable assigns numbers to outcomes; expectation E[X] = Σx·P(x) is the probability-weighted center — the long-run average per trial. Expectations are LINEAR: E[X+Y] = E[X]+E[Y] always, even under dependence — the one superpower that makes aggregate analysis tractable without independence assumptions.
prob-random-var-expectation.probe: A lottery: win 100 with p=0.01, lose 1 otherwise. Compute expected value per ticket. Then explain why E[X+Y]=E[X]+E[Y] holding WITHOUT independence lets you price a bundle of correlated bets easily.
rubric: linearity needs no independence: sum the individual expectations regardless of coupling
correlation affects the SPREAD of the bundle (variance), not its mean

prob-variance-sd.claim: Variance Var(X) = E[(X−μ)²] measures spread as squared distance from center; SD restores units. Variance ADDS for independent variables (Var(X+Y)=VarX+VarY) — but covariance terms appear under dependence, and they can be negative (hedging). Mean answers 'where', variance answers 'how much would it wobble'.
prob-variance-sd.probe: Two independent noise sources of ±0.1 A each add into a current measurement. Why is the combined spread ±0.14 (√2×0.1) rather than ±0.2? And what would make it worse than ±0.2?
rubric: independent variances add: 0.01+0.01=0.02 → SD=√0.02≈0.141 (accept 0.13–0.15) — partial cancellation between uncorrelated sources
worst case ±0.2 requires PERFECT positive correlation (same sign every time)
negative covariance (oppositely-signed errors) shrinks the sum below either alone — hedging

prob-common-distributions.claim: Distributions are process signatures: binomial = counting successes in n independent tries; Poisson = counting rare events per interval; exponential = waiting time between rare events; normal = accumulated small effects. Identify the PROCESS generating data and the distribution picks itself — fitting shapes blindly skips this step.
prob-common-distributions.probe: Match distributions and justify: (a) number of network packet errors per minute, (b) height across many people, (c) number of heads in 20 flips, (d) time until the next sensor dropout. Which pairing is most likely to fool someone and why?
rubric: (a) Poisson (rare events per interval), (b) normal (many additive factors), (c) binomial (fixed n trials), (d) exponential (waiting time)
(b) fools people: heights are NEAR-normal but truncated/bounded — real data rarely obeys exactly
identify mechanism first: count-per-trial → binomial, count-per-time → Poisson, wait-time → exponential

prob-clt.claim: The Central Limit Theorem: sums of many independent contributions look normal REGARDLESS of each contribution's shape — that's why averages of measurements behave bell-shaped while the underlying events may not be. The theorem licenses the normal's dominance in measurement error, and its limits (dependence, heavy tails, few terms) mark where bell-curve confidence breaks.
prob-clt.probe: Individual sensor glitches are wildly non-normal (spiky). Your weekly average of thousands of readings looks beautifully normal. Explain what CLT does here, then give two realistic conditions where the weekly average would NOT be normal.
rubric: CLT: the SUM/AVERAGE of many independent contributions converges to normal even when individuals aren't
breaks under dependence (glitches clustered by common cause) or heavy-tailed individuals (variance dominated by extremes)
practical upshot: bell shape of averages is earned by aggregation, not inherited from raw data

viz.hint: Roll N dice of ANY shape; histogram of their sum melts into a bell as N grows.

prob-law-large-numbers.claim: The Law of Large Numbers: sample averages converge to the true mean as n grows — but convergence is slow (√n) and says NOTHING about streaks. The gambler's fallacy ('heads is due') and hot-hand illusions both come from expecting short sequences to mirror long-run behavior. Small samples are noise-dominated, period.
prob-law-large-numbers.probe: A coin shows 5 heads in a row. A friend says 'tails is due — the law of averages demands it.' Fix the reasoning precisely: what LLN actually promises, what the next flip's probability remains, and how large n must roughly be before proportions settle within ±10%.
rubric: LLN describes convergence of the cumulative RATIO over many trials — no balancing force exists on short horizons
next flip stays P(heads)=0.5: coins have no memory

settling within ±10% needs n on the order of 100 (variance of proportion ~ 1/(4n)); 5 flips carry almost no information (accept any n from 50–400 with the 1/(4n) reasoning — the point is hundreds, not handfuls)

ode-flow-field-intuition.claim: An ODE x′ = f(x,t) is a velocity recipe: at every point of state space it tells you which way and how fast to move — a flow field. The solution isn't a formula first, it's a TRAJECTORY following the arrows. Sketching the field (nullclines, equilibria, arrow directions) predicts long-run behavior before any algebra.
ode-flow-field-intuition.probe: For x′ = x(1−x), sketch-in-words the flow field: what happens for 0<x<1, for x>1, and AT x=0 and x=1? Which points are equilibria and which is stable — all without solving anything.
rubric: 0<x<1: x′>0 → moves up toward 1; x>1: x′<0 → falls toward 1
equilibria where f=0: x=0 and x=1
x=1 stable (arrows converge), x=0 unstable (small positive x grows away) — logistic story told entirely by the field

viz.hint: Drop a ball on a slope-arrow landscape; watch it trace the solution curve through the field.

ode-flow-field-intuition.transfer_probe: A rumor spreads fastest when few have heard it and stalls when everyone has — the same x(1-x) shape. Sketch its flow field in words: which hearing-fractions grow, which shrink, where are the equilibria, and which one is stable?

ode-separable-basic.claim: Separable ODEs yield to the split-and-integrate procedure: herd all y's to one side, all x's to the other, integrate both, solve for y. It covers growth/decay, cooling, draining — and its limits matter: most ODEs are NOT separable, which is why numerical integration and linear-systems theory exist.
ode-separable-basic.probe: Solve dT/dt = −k(T−20) for coffee cooling from 90°, by separating. Then state the solution's shape in words and evaluate: at t→∞ what temperature results, and why does the equation guarantee it structurally?
rubric: separate: dT/(T−20) = −k dt → ln|T−20| = −kt+C → T = 20 + Ae^(−kt)
exponential approach: fast initially, slowing as gap shrinks
T→20 as t→∞ because driving term vanishes AT equilibrium (T−20=0 makes x′=0) — structure, not luck

practice.problem_frame: Solve a given separable ODE (cooling/draining/growth) by split-and-integrate and state the long-run behavior.
practice.discriminates_from: Integrating both sides without separating; forgetting the constant.
practice.verify: Substitute the solution back: does it reproduce the ODE? Check equilibrium limit.
error_bank: initial condition applied to the wrong branch

ode-linear-first-order.claim: First-order linear systems x′ = −λx solve to exponential decay/growth with time constant τ = 1/λ: the universal signature of processes whose rate is proportional to amount (RC discharge, cooling, sensor lag). Two such systems compose into cascaded lags — the workhorse model of thermal and electrical transients.
ode-linear-first-order.probe: An RC circuit discharges with RC = 2 s. Give the voltage decay law, the fraction remaining after one and three time constants, and explain why engineers quote '63%/37%' rather than half-lives in this context.
rubric: V = V₀e^(−t/RC): V/V₀ = e^(−t/τ)
after 1τ: 37% remains; after 3τ: ≈5% — the practical 'done' threshold (accept 4–6%; e⁻³≈4.98%)
time constants fit the proportional-rate structure directly; half-lives are the radioactive-counting convention of the same exponential

ode-second-order-oscillator.claim: Second-order systems m·x″ + c·x′ + k·x = 0 (mass-damper-spring) cover suspension, control loops, and RLC circuits alike. Damping ratio ζ decides personality: underdamped rings, critically damped returns fastest-without-overshoot, overdamped crawls. Natural frequency ωₙ = √(k/m) sets the clock; damping spends energy.
ode-second-order-oscillator.probe: You're tuning a door-closer (mass-spring-damper). Describe the three damping regimes by feel, name which one you want and why, and predict what happens to oscillation frequency if you stiffen the spring.
rubric: underdamped: overshoots and swings; critical: fastest smooth return; overdamped: sluggish no-bounce return
door closer wants near-critical damping — fast close without slam-bounce
stiffening k raises ωₙ=√(k/m): faster oscillation clock, higher pitch of any ringing

viz.hint: ζ slider morphs response between ringing sine, fastest-no-overshoot, and slow crawl.

ode-linear-systems-eigen.claim: Coupled linear systems x′ = Ax solve through eigenvalues: each eigenvector direction evolves independently as e^(λt). Stability reads straight off eigenvalues — negative real part decays (stable), positive grows (unstable), imaginary part rotates (oscillation). This is THE bridge from linear algebra to control theory: state-space stability is an eigenvalue census.
ode-linear-systems-eigen.probe: System x′ = Ax has eigenvalues −2±3i and +0.5. Describe the motion: which directions decay-and-spiral, which explodes, and what the overall fate of generic initial conditions is. What would you need to change for stability?
rubric: complex pair −2±3i: spiral inward (decay rate 2, angular speed 3 rad/s) in that eigenplane
+0.5 eigenvalue: exponential growth along its eigenvector — dominates eventually
generic trajectories end up racing out along the unstable eigendirection; fix requires making ALL eigenvalue real parts negative (feedback redesign)

viz.hint: Phase-plane with trajectories; toggle eigenvalues and watch spiral-in, spiral-out, saddle.

ode-stability-equilibria.claim: Equilibria are points where motion stops (f=0); their stability is decided LOCALLY by linearization — the Jacobian's eigenvalues at the point. Stable = perturbations shrink, unstable = grow, saddle = mixed. Linearization fails only at bifurcation boundaries, which is exactly where interesting behavior (switching, oscillation onset) lives.
ode-stability-equilibria.probe: For a pendulum, identify both equilibria and classify each via the linearization argument. Then explain why the inverted position is predicted unstable by eigenvalues, and give one example of behavior linearization CANNOT predict.
rubric: hanging-down in the undamped linearized ideal: Jacobian eigenvalues purely imaginary (center — neutral, oscillates); with any damping it becomes a stable spiral/focus — state the idealization; inverted: one positive real eigenvalue (unstable saddle)
linearization classifies LOCAL behavior near each equilibrium
cannot predict: global behavior far from equilibria, limit-cycle onset, and exact bifurcation points where classification flips

math-transform-laplace-preview.claim: The Laplace transform converts calculus problems into algebra: differentiation becomes multiplication by s, so ODEs become polynomial equations and transfer functions G(s) become readable spec sheets (poles = eigenvalue-like stability markers, gain = DC behavior). Control theory speaks this dialect — s-domain fluency is why PID tuning recipes work.
math-transform-laplace-preview.probe: In words: how does L{df/dt} = sF(s) − f(0) turn a differential equation into an algebraic one? Given a transfer function with poles at −1 and −3, state the system's stability and which pole governs the slowest transient.
rubric: transform replaces derivative operators with s-multipliers → ODE becomes polynomial in s, solved algebraically, inverse-transformed back
poles at negative reals → stable decaying exponentials
slowest transient set by pole nearest the imaginary axis: −1 (time constant 1 s vs 1/3 s)

math-prob-la-bridge.claim: Probability and linear algebra fuse in covariance structures: a covariance matrix encodes how random-vector components co-vary — diagonal entries are variances, off-diagonal correlations. Multivariate Gaussian ellipsoids, PCA finding max-variance directions (eigenvectors OF the covariance), and Kalman-filter gain updates are all 'eigen/projection thinking applied to uncertainty'.
math-prob-la-bridge.probe: Two sensors' errors are correlated (r=0.9). Draw-in-words the joint error cloud vs the r=0 case, explain what PCA would report as the first principal direction, and why fusing these two sensors yields less new information than two independent ones would.
rubric: r=0.9: elongated ellipse along the diagonal; r=0: round cloud
first principal component = major axis = top eigenvector of the covariance matrix (max-variance direction)
high correlation = redundant information: second sensor mostly re-measures the first's error, so fusion gain is small versus independent errors

viz.hint: Correlation slider deforms a scatter ellipse; PCA arrow snaps to the long axis.

capstone.claim: You can USE Mathematical Foundations — linear algebra, probability, and dynamics intuition in your own work, not just explain it.
capstone.probe: Build the thing. In your real repo, your real notes, your real argument — produce something that only works if you actually understand Mathematical Foundations — linear algebra, probability, and dynamics intuition. Your stated goal: The shared substrate under everything else in the vault: linear algebra powers state-space control, FOC's rotating transforms, and least-squares regression; probability powers sensor fusion, uncertainty analysis, and all of data-science-ai; ODE intuition powers every dynamics model from pendulum to QDD. This tree teaches the GEOMETRY first (transforms, projections, flow fields) with formulas as bookkeeping — each node cross-references where it lands in the mechatronics and DS trees. Threshold arcs: matrix-as-transform, Bayes inversion.. Ship it, then explain which concept made which decision.
rubric: the artifact exists and works (or the argument stands on its own)
names at least two concepts from this topic that DECIDED something in it
identifies where the model broke down or needed more than the topic gave

complex-euler-phasors.claim: Euler's formula e^{jθ} = cosθ + j sinθ turns rotation into algebra: multiplying by e^{jθ} rotates by θ. A sinusoid becomes a phasor — one complex number carrying magnitude and phase — so steady-state AC analysis is arithmetic, not trig identities. DFT bins are projections onto e^{-j2πkn/N} (negative frequency = opposite rotation; a real signal needs both, hence symmetric bins). Clarke/Park transforms are the same idea in motor control: a complex rotation into a frame that spins with the rotor.
complex-euler-phasors.probe: x(t) = 3cos(2t + π/4). Write it as Re{A e^{j2t}}: what are |A| and ∠A? Then: what does multiplying a phasor by e^{jπ/2} do geometrically, and why does the DFT of a REAL signal have mirror bins at +k and −k?
rubric: A = 3e^{jπ/4}: |A| = 3, angle π/4 (magnitude = amplitude, angle = phase shift)
×e^{jπ/2} = +90° rotation (cosine becomes negative sine — a quarter-cycle shift, not a scaling)
real-signal bins mirror because e^{+jθ} and e^{-jθ} are conjugates: opposite rotations whose imaginary parts cancel, leaving a real sum — one side alone would be complex

viz.hint: Rotating phasor with projection onto the real axis; flip rotation direction and watch the imaginary part change sign.

discrete-time-sampling.claim: Digital control sees the world in snapshots: a zero-order hold freezes u for a whole sample period T, so ẋ=Ax+Bu becomes x[k+1] = Ad x[k] + Bd u[k]. Stability moves from 'eigenvalues left of the axis' to 'eigenvalues inside the unit circle' via e^{λT}. Two bills come due: an EMA's cutoff is set by α AND T together (τ = −T/ln α — change Fs without retuning α and the cutoff silently moves), and every sample of computation/transport delay eats ωT radians of phase margin at crossover.
discrete-time-sampling.probe: Loop at 1 kHz, accel EMA α=0.98. You halve the rate to 500 Hz keeping α=0.98. What happens to the cutoff, and why? Second: one full sample of computation delay with a 100 Hz crossover — how much phase margin does it eat, and what is the fix?
rubric: cutoff drops ~2×: τ = −T/ln α doubles when T doubles (α fixes per-sample forgetting, T fixes what a sample means) — retune α = e^{−ωc T} for the new rate
delay eats ωT = 2π·100·0.001 ≈ 0.63 rad ≈ 36° of margin — usually fatal; fix by raising Fs, cutting the delay, or lowering crossover
stability test moved: continuous poles left-half-plane ↔ discrete poles inside unit circle (e^{λT} mapping)

viz.hint: Continuous step response vs ZOH staircase; slider on T while phase margin evaporates at fixed crossover.

calculus-intuition.claim: Calculus in mechatronics is two pictures, not epsilon-deltas: derivative = rate of change (position → velocity → acceleration, the slope of one signal graph), integral = accumulation (area under the curve; velocity → position). Every motor spec is a rate; every motion profile is an area.
calculus-intuition.probe: A motor spins with angular velocity ω that ramps linearly from 0 to 100 rad/s over 2 seconds, then holds at 100 for another 2 seconds. Sketch ω(t), then sketch θ(t) and α(t) qualitatively. What is the total angle after 4 s?
rubric: ω(t) is a ramp then a plateau
θ(t) is quadratic during the ramp (area under a triangle) then linear (area under a rectangle)
α(t) is constant during the ramp, zero after
total angle = ½·2·100 + 2·100 = 300 rad
